title: Implement a trie, also called a prefix tree, supporting inserting a word, searching for a complete word, and checking whether any word starts with a given prefix. Explain the Trie pattern, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Implement a Trie (Prefix Tree with Insert, Search, and StartsWith)

s1_definition.oneliner: A trie stores characters along edges so every key operation costs only the length of the key, and the Trie pattern uses this for prefix-based lookups.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Trie pattern** – a design pattern using a prefix tree to efficiently handle word insertion, exact lookup, and prefix matching.
- **Edge characters** – each edge in the tree carries one character; a root-to-node path spells a prefix.
- **End-of-word flag** – a boolean on each node marking whether a complete word terminates there.
- **Shared prefixes** – words sharing a prefix share the same initial path, saving space.
- **Key-length operations** – insert, search, and startsWith all run in O(L) time where L is the key length.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India stores a large set of registered merchant names and wants to look up names and check prefixes quickly as a teller types. A trie stores shared prefixes once, so RELIANCE and RELIABLE share the same early branch, making both exact lookups and prefix autocomplete fast.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Trie Pattern: Merchant Name Lookup

  After inserting: RELIANCE, RELIABLE, HDFC

         [root]
        /       \
      R           H
      |           |
      E           D
      |           |
      L           F
      |           |
      I           C*
      |
      A
     / \
    N   B
    |   |
    C   L
    |   |
    E*  E*

  * = isWord = true

  Search "RELIANCE":  R->E->L->I->A->N->C->E -> isWord=true -> TRUE
  Search "RELI":      R->E->L->I -> isWord=false -> FALSE
  Prefix "RELI":      R->E->L->I -> node exists -> TRUE

  Autocomplete "RELI":
  Walk to I node, DFS:
    A -> N -> C -> E* (collect "RELIANCE")
    A -> B -> L -> E* (collect "RELIABLE")
  Result: ["RELIANCE", "RELIABLE"]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Trie pattern uses a prefix tree to handle word insertion, exact-word lookup, and prefix matching, all in time proportional to the key length. Each edge carries one character, each root-to-node path spells a prefix, and words sharing a prefix share the same initial nodes. The isWord flag on each node distinguishes a complete word from a prefix that happens to pass through.

Insert walks character by character creating missing children and sets isWord on the last node. Search does the same walk and succeeds only when the path exists and isWord is true. StartsWith succeeds whenever the path exists, regardless of isWord. The shared traversal helper makes the code clean and the three operations differ by just one condition.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used the Trie pattern to power a merchant name lookup with autocomplete. A teller typing "RELI" instantly saw matching merchants, and exact lookups confirmed whether a name was registered. The trie handled 50,000 merchant names with prefix queries in microseconds.

The senior insight is knowing when to use the Trie pattern versus a HashMap. Tries win for prefix queries, autocomplete, and lexicographic iteration. HashMaps win for pure exact-match lookups with lower memory. In production, compressed tries (radix trees) merge single-child chains, and frequency counts per node enable ranked autocomplete.

Remember one sentence: The Trie pattern stores characters on edges, uses isWord to distinguish complete words from prefixes, and gives O(key length) operations for insert, search, and prefix matching.

---

keyPoints: The Trie pattern uses a prefix tree for word insertion, exact lookup, and prefix matching.
Shared prefixes are stored once, saving space when many words share leading characters.
The isWord flag is the critical distinction between search (requires true) and startsWith (ignores it).
All three operations run in O(key length) time, independent of how many words are stored.
Autocomplete walks to the prefix node and DFS-collects all words below it.
In production, compressed tries (radix trees) reduce per-node overhead for long shared prefixes.
